doc.title: Dawoud Sabu Adeyola interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, January 30, 2025

title: Closing: Louis Armstrong epiphany and goodbyes
summary: Thanks, his mother showing him Louis Armstrong on TV, musings on divine gift, and goodbyes.

story.theme_name: Thanks and goodbyes: closing the interview
story.community_name: Closing thanks and goodbyes at the end of the interview

blocks.x: Well this has been a fascinating conversation. I’m so glad we had the opportunity. I want to thank you for your time and your — how well you speak about your music and everything that goes with it.

I apologize for going on and on sometimes. You know. But as you can see I probably need to publish my books because as you can see I have a lot to say about it, I’ve got deep feelings about it. It’s been basically a love affair. And I’ll tell you another funny story before we go — I know we’ve got a time element. But you know when my mother first came to me and said she wanted me to take music lessons I was against it. You know? I was about seven, eight, something like that. And I didn’t want to take music lessons. I didn’t want to take piano lessons. And she said, “Why not?” I said, “Because the music is for girls.” And she said, “Why would you say that?” I said, “Because all the musicians I see, like in church, they were my aunts and my cousins, but they were all girls.” She said, “No, the best musicians in the world are men.” And I was like, “Where are they? I ain’t never seen none.” So one day I was out in the yard playing and my sister came, my older sister came and said, “Mama says come in right now. Come, quick, come.” And so she grabbed me and drug me in the living room, and she said, my mom said, “Look.” There’s a TV on you know, there’s Louis Armstrong. Louis Armstrong man, with his trumpet in one hand, a hankie in the other hand. And he’s clean, he’s got a tuxedo on. She said, “He’s the best in the world. There you go. He’s the best.” I said, “Oh, really?” So that changed my thinking. And then of course then I wanted a trumpet. So anyway that’s part of my metamorphosis.
Terrific. I’ve had a couple — I didn’t know the word but now I do — epiphanies myself like that.
Epiphany. Yeah. Yeah. And I don’t know how she knew it but she knew, back then in the ‘50s, she said, “He’s the best musician in the whole world.” You know? And now over a © Fillius Jazz Archive -21-

hundred years after his birth, or fifty or so years after his death, and pretty much everybody agrees yup, he’s the guy. Louis — nobody — like Miles said one time, he said, “There’s nothing we can play that Louis hasn’t played already.” I’m like wow.
Those Hot 5 and Hot 7 records were recorded like a hundred years ago.

Yeah. Well see that’s why, Monk that’s why we know that this thing is — the mind, it’s divinely revealed. It’s not really from us. It’s something other-worldly. You know like Art Blakey said, “Music is a gift, you know, it’s from the creator to the artist, to the artist in split second timing.” And that’s something that is unrehearsed, is unplanned. We don’t know, was it Sonny Rollins or Coltrane one time, somebody came back stage and showed him some music and said, “What do you think about this?” And he said, “Oh it looks interesting but it’s just too difficult, I never could play it.” And they told Coltrane, “No, this is your solo on ‘Blue Trane.’” He said, “I played that?” Yup. There you go.
Somebody transcribed the whole thing you know. Anyway thanks so much, I really appreciate it.
All right, thanks for your time, I’ll pause our recording and then we’ll say our good-byes. Appreciate it.
Absolutely. Thank you. © Fillius Jazz Archive -22-
